query: In conventional alloys, loss of toughness has long been associated with grain-boundary segregation and brittle grain-boundary precipitation. By contrast, compositionally complex high-entropy alloys can suppress rapid grain coarsening and deleterious intermetallic formation and have shown favorable strength–ductility combinations and resistance to high-temperature softening and low-temperature embrittlement. These findings do not establish what governs possible toughness degradation in an initially single-phase high-entropy alloy. Under the constraint of retaining a compositionally complex alloy suitable for demanding engineering service, what testable mechanistic hypothesis explains whether and why brittle behavior emerges? Specify a controlled comparison that would distinguish the hypothesis from conventional-alloy expectations, predicted observations relative to the initial baseline, its service and loading boundaries, supporting prior evidence, and a decisive falsification outcome.

generation.hypothesis: In a single‐phase high–entropy alloy, even in the absence of the coarse, intergranular precipitates seen in conventional alloys, the gradual diffusion and segregation of trace impurities (e.g., oxygen or nitrogen) during prolonged high–temperature service lead to the formation of nanoscale, compositionally distinct clusters at grain boundaries. These nanoclusters act as local stress concentrators that promote brittle crack initiation under service loads.
generation.material_initial_state: An initially single–phase, compositionally complex high–entropy alloy with a uniform solid solution and minimal impurity segregation.
generation.intervention: Subject the alloy to controlled aging treatments at elevated service temperatures while varying the level of trace impurities (e.g., comparing high–purity versus intentionally doped with small amounts of oxygen/nitrogen).
generation.conditions: High temperature (service temperature range where diffusion is active), under mechanical load conditions (e.g., during tensile tests) to probe toughness, in inert atmospheres to avoid extrinsic oxidation.
generation.structural_mediator: Nanoscale impurity–induced clusters forming preferentially at grain boundaries.
generation.mechanism: During thermal exposure, even low levels of impurities diffuse and accumulate at grain boundaries; due to the high–entropy stabilization, these clusters do not develop into coarse precipitates but instead remain as nanoclusters that locally disrupt the bonding environment and act as stress concentrators, reducing the ability to accommodate plastic deformation and thus precipitating a brittle response.
generation.predicted_outcome: Samples aged in the presence of trace impurities will exhibit reduced toughness and earlier crack initiation at grain boundaries relative to high–purity samples, despite both maintaining a single–phase structure. Fractography should reveal nanometer–scale heterogeneities at grain boundaries correlating with brittle fracture paths.
generation.baseline: The initial high–entropy alloy exhibits a uniform single–phase microstructure with favorable strength–ductility trade–offs and no evidence of nanocluster formation at grain boundaries.
generation.boundary: The effect is predicted under service conditions where thermal activation allows impurity diffusion (moderate to high temperatures) and under loading conditions that engage grain boundary mediated deformation. The hypothesis may not apply at low temperatures where diffusion is negligible or at very high strain rates where dynamic effects dominate.
generation.uncertainty: The precise kinetics of nanocluster formation and the quantitative impact on toughness are uncertain, as is the threshold impurity level required to induce a measurable brittle transition. Other factors such as dynamic amorphization might interact with impurity effects, complicating the relationship.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of the same high–entropy alloy: one processed with high–purity feedstock and another with a controlled addition of trace impurities (oxygen/nitrogen). Subject both sets to identical thermal aging treatments at a service–relevant temperature. Perform mechanical testing (e.g., tensile or fracture toughness tests) and detailed microstructural analysis (e.g., high–resolution TEM and APT) focusing on grain boundary chemistry.
measurements: Nanoindentation to evaluate local mechanical properties
Grain boundary microstructure and chemical composition via TEM/APT
Crack initiation and propagation location via fractography
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the impurity–doped samples do not show any statistically significant reduction in toughness or evidence of nanoscale grain boundary segregation relative to the high–purity samples after aging, or if similar brittle behavior is observed regardless of impurity level, the hypothesized mechanism is falsified.

cited_evidence.text:
Origin of age softening in the refractory high-entropy alloys

Abstract: AbstractRefractory high-entropy alloys (RHEAs) are emerging materials with potential for use under extreme conditions. As a newly developed material system, a comprehensive understanding of their long-term stability under potential service temperatures remains to be established. This study examined a titanium-vanadium-niobium-tantalum alloy, a promising RHEA known for its superior high-temperature strength and room-temperature ductility. Using a combination of advanced analytical microscopies, Calculation of Phase Diagrams (CALPHAD) software, and nanoindentation, we investigated the evolution of its microstructure and mechanical properties upon aging at 700°C. Trace interstitials such as oxygen and nitrogen, initially contributing to solid solution strengthening, promote phase segregation during thermal aging. As a result of the depletion of solute interstitials within the metal matrix, a progressive softening is observed in the alloy as a function of aging time.
